questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl presented with 5 days of low-grade fevers and malaise and one day of rash on her face and trunk. Her pediatrician advised supportive care, and the rash and fevers resolved over the next few days. Her 15-year-old foster brother has sickle cell disease.
questions.lead_in: If he were to have infection with the same agent, he would be particularly at risk for what complication?
questions.explanation: Aplastic anemia In patients with hemoglobinopathies, parvovirus can cause pure red cell aplasia by driving persistent lysis of red blood cell precursors. Pregnant women are also particularly at risk for severe complications with parvovirus infection, including miscarriage, intrauterine fetal death, and hydrops fetalis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q31

questions.stem: A 20-week pregnant woman presented to antenatal clinic 1 day after an exposure to a child with slapped cheek at the school where she works. She was asymptomatic. Investigations: Parvovirus B19 IgM not detected Parvovirus B19 IgG not detected
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Advise her that she cannot return to work
Refer for serial ultrasound scan monitoring
Repeat parvovirus B19 serology at 4 weeks following exposure
Request serologic testing for toxoplasma, rubella, and CMV

questions.explanation: Repeat parvovirus B19 serology at 4 weeks following exposure Serologic testing shows the patient to be susceptible to parvovirus B19. A significant proportion of infections with parvovirus B19 are asymptomatic; therefore guidance recommends re-testing at 4 weeks postcontact. If her serologic tests at this time remain negative she can be reassured that she has not had the infection. However, she should be advised that she remains susceptible to infection.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q13

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child had been unwell for several days with a mild fever, coryza and malaise, and flushed facies. On examination there was a rash over both arms. It was mildly pruritic, nontender, and blanching.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Erythema infectiosum Erythema infectiosum or parvovirus B19 is usually diagnosed clinically in children with the classic appearance of malar rash: the slapped cheek rash. In some cases, a further rash develops predominantly on the arms and legs, which is described as lacy in appearance and may take several weeks to resolve fully. The rash of rubella, measles, and human herpesvirus 6 (exanthem subitum) are characteristically widespread, generalized maculopapular exanthems. (Image from Kadambari S, Segal S. Acute viral exanthems. Medicine. 2017;45(12):788–793.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q12

questions.stem: A 43-year-old man presented with 4 weeks of worsening fatigue and dyspnea on exertion. He denied fevers, chills, weight loss, or cough. He was the primary carer for his 4-year-old nephew who had had a febrile illness with a facial rash 2 months earlier. The patient was known to have HIV and was not on antiretroviral therapy. On examination there was conjunctival pallor but no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Investigations: CD4 count 45 cells/μL HIV viral load 14,350 copies/mL Total white cell count 4300 cells/μL (3500–10,500) Hemoglobin 7,2 g/dL (13.5–17.5) Reticulocyte percentage 1.2% (0.77%–2.36%) Haptoglobin 75 mg/dL (30–200) Antinuclear antibody test negative Direct Coombs test negative Bone marrow biopsy showed overall hypocellular marrow with giant pronormoblasts seen.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Intravenous immunoglobulin The presentation of severe anemia without evidence of hemolysis and an inappropriately low reticulocyte count is suggestive of pure red cell aplasia. In advanced AIDS patients, parvovirus B19 is a well-recognized cause of this condition, with characteristic bone marrow findings as in this case. Parvovirus B19 causes Fifth disease in children, usually manifesting with febrile illness and slapped cheek rash. Diagnosis is usually confirmed with parvovirus B19 PCR, and the treatment of choice for pure red cell aplasia in advanced AIDS is IVIG.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q22

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman presented with mild fever, malaise, and myalgia 1 week after her 5-year-old son developed a malar rash after a few days of fever and coryzal symptoms (see image). She was usually fit and well. She had an intrauterine device in situ and did not take any regular medications. She had no known allergies. She had been born and brought up in Albania and had moved to the UK at 18 years of age. She was concerned about the possible complications.
questions.lead_in: What complication is she most likely to develop?
questions.explanation: Rheumatoid-like polyarthritis Accompanying joint symptoms are rare in children but may be severe in adults, more often in women. These consist of an acute, symmetric, rheumatoid-like polyarthritis which usually improves within 2 weeks but occasionally may persist for months. (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q45

questions.question: PM 11. What is the most likely infectious cause of the following congenital findings? periventricular calcifications (0.5); cutaneous scarring (0.5); heart failure (0.5); Osteitis (0.5); Cataracts (0.5)

parts.text: Identify the infectious cause for each congenital finding

cohort_answer.text: Periventricular calcifications - CMV (widespread/intracranial calcifications more suggest Toxoplasmosis). Cutaneous scarring - VZV. Heart failure - Parvovirus (>>>Rubella). Osteitis - Syphilis (saber shin). Cataracts - Rubella.

questions.question: Regarding parvovirus B19:

parts.text: List FOUR common clinical syndromes.
By what route is this virus transmitted in humans?
What is the risk of congenital (mother to child) transmission if a pregnant woman is infected?
When is an immunocompetent patient most infectious?

questions.model_answer:
a) Four common clinical syndromes: (1) erythema infectiosum/fifth disease (children), (2) polyarthropathy syndrome (adults), (3) transient aplastic crisis (patients with underlying hemolytic disease, e.g., sickle cell disease), (4) hydrops fetalis/congenital anemia (fetal infection); (chronic pure red cell aplasia in immunocompromised patients is also accepted).
b) Transmission: primarily respiratory route (respiratory secretions/droplet), also via blood and blood products and vertically (transplacental, mother to fetus).
c) Congenital transmission risk: overall excess fetal loss is low (~9%), and risk is essentially confined to infection in the first 20 weeks of pregnancy; most infected fetuses have no long-term abnormalities, though hydrops fetalis can occur in a minority.
d) Most infectious period: immunocompetent patients are viremic and infectious during the prodromal phase, before the rash of erythema infectiosum appears — once the rash (immune complex-mediated) develops, high-titer viremia is no longer present and the patient is not considered infectious.

questions.question: 24F nurse 15 weeks pregnant looking after patient with parvovirus.

parts.text: A. Gives nurses' table of serology and asks what the management should be.
B. What 3 fetal complications can be expected if congenital parvo?

cohort_answer.text:
If serology negative -> monitor for symptoms. If converts -> monitor closely, fetal monitoring. If serology positive -> protective. IgM-/IgG+: Past infection, protected. IgM+/IgG-or+: Acute infection, U/S/MCA dopplers q1-2 weeks for 12 weeks after infection. IgM-/IgG-: Susceptible, avoid exposure
Hydrops fetalis; Myocarditis; Anemia; IUGR; Death

parts.text: 4 common manifestations of parvovirus B19
Route of transmission
Risk to fetus if mom is infected in pregnancy?
What do you tell mom about work (she works in a day care)
What to do if in the setting of an outbreak?

cohort_answer.text: A) Erythema infectiosum or "fifth disease" - nonspecific viral prodrome (fever, coryza, headache, mild nausea/diarrhea) followed by slapped cheek rash then maculopapular lacy exanthem. Polyarthropathy syndrome (adults, symmetrical). PPGSS - papular purpuric gloves-and-socks syndrome (painful pruritic papules, petechiae, symmetrical on hands & feet). Chronic erythroid hypoplasia (pure red cell aplasia). Transient aplastic crisis. Congenital infections - fetal hydrops, IUGR, death. B) Droplets, vertical transmission. C) Fetal death rate 6.3% overall in pregnancies (highest if infection occurs in first 20 weeks GA, minimal risk after 20 weeks); fetal hydrops - 4% risk. D) Do not exclude from work: outbreaks widespread in community/school/daycares, high prevalence of B19 infection, low incidence of adverse effects on fetus, avoidance of work does not eliminate risk of infection/exposure. E) Droplet precautions if aplastic crisis, PPGSS, immunosuppressed with chronic infection for duration of admission. Transient aplastic crisis only requires precautions for 7 days (or until reticulocyte count recovered to at least 2%). No precautions needed for fetal hydrops. For erythema infectiosum: routine precautions as no longer infectious once rash appears.

parts.text: A. What are the syndromes associated with parvovirus (5)? B. Are they acute or chronic? C. What host is typically affected by each syndrome (Fetus, Child, Normal Adult, IC)
D. Route of transmission
E. Risk to fetus if mom infected in pregnancy?

cohort_answer.text:
A/B/C: Syndrome | Chronicity | Patient | Info. Fifth disease (erythema infectiosum) | Acute | Child | Fever + slapped cheek. Hydrops fetalis | Chronic | Fetus | Hydrops fetalis. Fetal loss | Chronic | Fetus | Fetal loss. Polyarthropathy | Chronic | Adult | 2 weeks post infection, symmetric, small jts. Papulopurpuric gloves-and-socks syndrome (PPGS) | Acute | Adult | Painful edema and erythema to extremities that progress to petechiae and purpura. Transient aplastic anemia | Acute | Sicklers | In patients with chronic hemolytic disorders. Pure red cell aplasia | Chronic | IC | Anemia

D: Respiratory droplet. Blood transfusion. Vertical. Transplant

E: 30-50% of fetuses from infected, previously seronegative, mothers will become infected

parts.text: Name 4 common manifestations of this infection (2)
How is it transmitted (0.5)
What is the overall likelihood of vertical transmission if infected during pregnancy (0.5)
When is an immunocompetent person considered most infectious (0.5)

cohort_answer.text: Manifestations: PPGSS - papular-purpuric 'gloves and socks' syndrome; Erythema infectiosum (5th disease); Hydrops fetalis/congenital anemia; Pure red cell aplasia; Polyarthropathy Syndrome; Transient aplastic crisis. Transmission: Spread through droplets. Vertical transmission rate: 30%; fetal death rate 2-6% overall (highest if infection in first 20 weeks GA, minimal risk after 20 weeks - Redbook); fetal hydrops 4% risk. Most infectious period: Before rash develops, no longer infectious once rash develops; incubation period 4-21 days; 1 week after onset of aplastic crisis; keep inpatients with PPGSS or immunocompromised on droplet for entire admission (literature does not specify how long someone is infectious prior to rash developing)
